device.category: self-contained analogue 'compact electronic music studio': three oscillators, treatments, pin-matrix patching, joystick, speakers
device.based_on: Original design by David Cockerell for EMS, introduced 1969; the source of the Synthi A and AKS.

sources.title: VCS3 Compact Electronic Music Studio Users Manual (EMS)
sources.note: Scanned; read by OCR at 300 dpi. Full specification with dial calibration tables and control sensitivities, a matrix tutorial with labelled matrix diagram, a description of every device, external equipment and maintenance sections, 15 specimen patch sheets (knob settings drawn as dials, not readable by OCR) and a glossary. The matrix layout (separate rows for each Osc 1 and Osc 2 waveform) is the Mk 1's.

architecture.synthesis_note: subtractive at heart, with ring modulation and FM by patching audio into control inputs
architecture.polyphony_mode: none as such: three free-running oscillators that can sound together as a chord; no keyboard (EMS DK1 or DK2 optional)
architecture.summary: Not a keyboard synthesizer but a small studio. Nothing is connected until pins are placed in a 16 x 16 matrix: rows are the outputs of every device (three oscillators' waveforms, noise, two input amplifiers, filter, envelope trapezoid and signal, ring modulator, reverb, joystick X and Y) and columns are inputs, signal inputs on the left (meter, two output amplifiers, envelope, ring modulator A and B, reverb, filter) and control inputs on the right (three oscillator frequencies, envelope decay, reverb mix, filter frequency, two output amplifier levels). Each pin holds a 2.7 kohm resistor, so several pins in one column mix, and any output can drive any input, signal or control. Oscillator 1 gives sine (with a shape control) and ramp; Oscillators 2 and 3 give square/pulse and triangle/ramp from one shape control; Oscillator 3 runs from about one cycle a minute to 500 Hz and is the main control source. The filter doubles as a sine oscillator. The envelope shaper is a self-repeating trapezoid generator with its own VCA. Two output amplifiers with voltage-controlled level, tone and pan feed internal speakers and rear outputs. A joystick gives two control voltages.

modules.name: Oscillator 1
modules.description: Sine and ramp outputs, each with its own level, on rows 1 and 2. The shape control acts on the sine output only: at its centre point it is a pure sine, either side it distorts towards a rectified shape. 1 Hz to 10 kHz on the slow-motion dial, 1.5 octaves per major division. Frequency control on column I.

modules.name: Oscillator 2
modules.description: Square and triangle outputs, each with its own level, on rows 3 and 4. One shape control acts on both: off centre the triangle becomes a ramp and the square a pulse, so changing one changes the other. At the extremes the pulse vanishes and the output is effectively DC. Same range as Oscillator 1. Frequency control on column J.

modules.name: Oscillator 3
modules.description: As Oscillator 2 but about 20 times slower: from more than 40 seconds per cycle to 500 Hz. Intended mainly as a control source (the role an LFO plays elsewhere), audible only at the top of its range, roughly dial 7 to 10. Rows 5 and 6; frequency control on column K.

modules.name: Noise Generator
modules.description: Not voltage controlled. Colour control from dark (low-pass) through white (centre) to light (high-pass), and a level, on row 7. Takes 20 to 30 seconds to start after power-on.

properties.colour_circuit: passive balance between a low-pass and a high-pass network of the same turnover frequency (inferred from a DIY circuit described as derived from the VCS3)

modules.name: Input Amplifier 1
modules.description: Brings an external signal or control voltage onto row 8. Fed by the MIC 1 jack, the HI LEVEL INPUT 1 jack (DC coupled, so usable for control voltages) or a low-level DC input on the KEYBOARD socket, one at a time. Voltage gain of 2, inverting.

modules.name: Input Amplifier 2
modules.description: Brings an external signal or control voltage onto row 9. Fed by the MIC 2 jack, the HI LEVEL INPUT 2 jack (DC coupled, so usable for control voltages) or a low-level DC input on the KEYBOARD socket, one at a time. Voltage gain of 2, inverting.

modules.name: Ring Modulator
modules.description: Transformerless IC ring modulator: output only when both inputs (columns E and F) carry signal, sum and difference frequencies with the inputs suppressed. AC coupled, so slow inputs are differentiated and DC has no effect. One output level control, row 13.

modules.name: Filter/Oscillator
modules.description: Low-pass filter whose RESPONSE control narrows it into a resonant peak (high-Q at about 5 to 6) and then, a little beyond, into a low-distortion sine oscillator, the purest sine in the instrument. Cut-off falls at 12 dB in the first octave and 18 dB per octave beyond. 5 Hz to 10 kHz. Signal in on column H, frequency control on column N, output on row 10.

properties.version_note: 12/18 dB slope applies to units sold 1969 to 1974; EMS changed the filter to 24 dB/octave in 1974 (Sound On Sound)

modules.name: Envelope Shaper
modules.description: A trapezoid generator with its own amplifier. Four times (attack, on, decay, off) form a cycle that repeats on its own, up to about 60 Hz with all times at minimum and down to about 20 seconds per cycle; with OFF turned past about 5 to 7 the cycle stops after each decay and waits for the ATTACK button or a keyboard trigger. Signal in on column D comes out shaped on row 12; the control shape itself is on row 11 (the trapezoid). Decay time is voltage controlled from column L, which also changes the repetition rate. A lamp shows bright for attack and on, dim for decay and off.

trigger.source: ATTACK button or Jones socket pin 5

modules.name: Reverberation Unit
modules.description: Twin spring line (25 and 30 ms delays, over 2 seconds' reverberation) with a MIX control from dry to almost all spring, voltage controlled from column M (-2 V dry, +2 V full). Signal in on column G, output on row 14. Sensitive to knocks and to acoustic feedback from the internal speakers.

modules.name: Joystick
modules.description: Two potentiometers at right angles, moved in a square. Each axis has a RANGE control; output is 0 V at centre, negative down and left, positive up and right, up to plus or minus 2 V. Horizontal on row 15, vertical on row 16. Effective on control columns; on signal columns only the ring modulator 'bowing' trick uses it.

modules.name: Meter and scope tap
modules.description: 1 mA moving-coil meter on column A. CONTROL VOLTAGES: centre-zero DC, plus or minus 1 V. SIGNAL LEVELS: left-zero AC, 4 V p-p full scale. The SCOPE jack is connected to the same column, so column A is also a third route out of the matrix.

modules.name: Output Amplifier 1
modules.description: Voltage-controlled output amplifier: signal in on column B, level control on column O. The large level knob is itself a control voltage, so with nothing on the control column the signal only appears at about half travel, and added control can make the signal impossible to cut. Bass and treble roll-off filter, flat at 5. Feeds the internal speaker (through its muting switch), the headphones and, through its PAN control, the signal outputs. The CONTROL OUTPUT 1 jack taps column B before the amplifier, DC coupled.

modules.name: Output Amplifier 2
modules.description: Voltage-controlled output amplifier: signal in on column C, level control on column P. The large level knob is itself a control voltage, so with nothing on the control column the signal only appears at about half travel, and added control can make the signal impossible to cut. Bass and treble roll-off filter, flat at 5. Feeds the internal speaker (through its muting switch), the headphones and, through its PAN control, the signal outputs. The CONTROL OUTPUT 2 jack taps column C before the amplifier, DC coupled.

modules.name: Outputs and speakers
modules.description: Two 1 W amplifiers and 5-inch internal speakers (non-panning), the stereo headphone socket (non-panning, high level), and the L and R signal outputs (panned).

electrical.crosstalk_note: small HF crosstalk to open inputs, about 12 dB less once an input is in use

patch_matrix.note: Rows carry device outputs and columns device inputs; the manual marks signal inputs with round boxes and control inputs with square boxes. Pins in the same column sum; pins in the same row distribute one output to several inputs. The matrix is unbuffered, so adding pins or changing output levels alters other connections. Any row can go to any column: audio into control columns gives FM or AM, and control into signal columns is mostly ineffective except at the AC-coupled ring modulator. Each row's level_param is the knob that scales that output before it reaches the matrix, and each control column's offset_param is the manual knob the pinned voltages add to; the panel prints the row number or column letter beside each one. Signal columns have no offset; their module's panel heading carries the column letter (D envelope, E and F ring modulator, G reverb, H filter). This is the Mk 1 layout: separate rows for each Osc 1 and Osc 2 waveform, no output channel rows, meter on column A (confirmed by Portabella), and row 16 is the joystick only.

example_patches.name: Swept coloured noise (Specimen Patch 1)
example_patches.source: manual Section III and Section VII sheet 1
example_patches.description: Noise through the filter and envelope shaper to both outputs. Osc 1 ramp and Osc 2 triangle, tuned close to beat, modulate the envelope decay; Osc 3 triangle sweeps the filter; the joystick controls both output levels. Variants: L1, L3, N5.

example_patches.name: Ring modulator octave
example_patches.description: Osc 1 sine and the self-oscillating filter, tuned to unison, into the ring modulator: an octave above. Retuning Osc 1 an octave down gives one note an octave below and its twelfth.

example_patches.name: Joystick 'bowing'
example_patches.description: Oscillators 1 and 2 into ring mod input A and the joystick's vertical axis into input B. Because the modulator is AC coupled, sound appears only while the stick moves: bow up and down, change pitch left and right.

example_patches.name: Bell tones
example_patches.description: Rich ring modulation filtered, struck by the envelope shaper and reverberated; the joystick retunes both oscillators.

example_patches.name: Filter extracts harmonics
example_patches.description: A low Osc 1 ramp through the filter while an Osc 3 rising ramp sweeps cut-off; the harmonics sound one by one.

example_patches.name: Amplitude swing between channels
example_patches.description: Osc 1 to both outputs, with Osc 2 and Osc 3, both slow and slightly out of step, on the two output amplifier levels.

example_patches.name: Ring-modulated clangs
example_patches.description: Ring modulator into the repeating envelope shaper, then reverb; the joystick changes the clang. The manual prints the envelope pin as B13; read as D13.

colours.meaning: mains on; envelope cycle state by brightness

behaviours.name: Nothing sounds until pinned
behaviours.rule: There is no default patch. Every route is a pin, and every patch must end at column B or C (or both) to be heard. Many settings produce silence: a sub- or supersonic oscillator, a level at zero, an output level below half way, a muted speaker.

behaviours.name: Resistive, unbuffered matrix
behaviours.rule: Each pin is a 2.7 kohm resistor into a 10 kohm input, so pins in one column sum, and every extra pin or level change slightly alters the others. Pin tolerance matters: two white pins carrying the same pitch voltage to two oscillators can make them track differently, which is what the red precision pins are for. Several pins in column A join their signals together.

behaviours.name: Signal and control are the same thing
behaviours.rule: Any row can feed any column. Audio into a control column gives FM (oscillators, filter) or AM (output amplifiers); slow sources into control columns give vibrato, sweeps and pan. The manual's own idioms: Osc 3 ramp on Osc 1 frequency for rising note patterns, Osc 2 and Osc 3 ramps summed into a staircase for scales, circular modulation between oscillators for pseudo-random patterns.

behaviours.name: Control voltage scaling
behaviours.rule: Not 1 V/octave. Through a pin: Osc 1 and 2 at 0.32 V/octave, Osc 3 at 0.26 V/octave, the filter at 0.2 V/octave, envelope decay doubles per 0.4 V. Through an input amplifier (gain 2) an external voltage needs half as much: 0.16 V/octave for Osc 1 and 2. Reverb mix runs from -2 V (dry) to +2 V (full). Joystick and range controls set intervals by ear, and an interval set at one pitch should hold at others. The input amplifiers invert, and the oscillators rise in pitch as their control voltage goes negative, so a conventional positive-going pitch voltage plays the right way round through an input amplifier but backwards if pinned in directly (Digitana).

behaviours.name: Envelope shaper cycle
behaviours.rule: Attack, on, decay and off run in a loop. With all four at minimum it buzzes at about 50 to 60 Hz; with attack, on and decay at 10 and off at half it repeats about every 20 seconds. Turning OFF past roughly 5 to 7 stops it after each decay, waiting for the ATTACK button (which holds ON while pressed) or a keyboard trigger. Attack longer than on makes decay start early, for gentle undulation. Decay control voltage (column L) changes both note length and repetition rate.

behaviours.name: Inverted trapezoid
behaviours.rule: The trapezoid runs from -3 V when ON to +3 V when OFF. Applied to an output amplifier level it therefore fades the signal during attack and restores it during decay: an inverted envelope. Applied to an oscillator it bends pitch through the note.

behaviours.name: Filter as oscillator
behaviours.rule: RESPONSE 0 is low-pass; about 5 to 6 is a sharp resonator; a little further it oscillates as a pure sine, and continues to oscillate to the right. The oscillation point varies with frequency. While oscillating it still filters, so a noise input gives howling wind. Its frequency control then works like an oscillator's.

behaviours.name: AC-coupled ring modulator
behaviours.rule: Output exists only when both inputs carry signal, and DC is ignored: slow inputs pass only their changes. That makes it a switch (remove one input), an octave doubler (same sine into both inputs), and with the joystick on one input a 'bow' that sounds only while the stick moves.

behaviours.name: Output amplifier level is a control voltage
behaviours.rule: The large level knob biases a VCA rather than attenuating. With nothing on its control column the signal appears around half travel; with control pinned, the knob's lower half backs the control off, and some settings cannot be silenced.

behaviours.name: Three ways out of the matrix
behaviours.rule: CONTROL OUTPUTS 1 and 2 tap columns B and C before the output amplifiers, DC coupled, and SCOPE taps column A. Pinning a control source to B or C is how a control voltage leaves the VCS3; SCOPE can feed a signal back in through an input amplifier.

behaviours.name: Noise warm-up
behaviours.rule: The noise generator does not start for 20 to 30 seconds after power-on.

behaviours.name: Reverb overload and feedback
behaviours.rule: The springs' output varies 10 to 1 with frequency, so peaks can overload even at modest average levels, especially with slowly swept tones. Acoustic feedback can occur through the internal speakers; reduce MIX slightly. Knocking the cabinet excites the springs.

behaviours.name: Panel legends map knobs to the matrix
behaviours.rule: Every source has a level knob numbered with its matrix row (1 to 14; the joystick RANGE knobs are 15 and 16), and every control column has a manual knob lettered with its column (I to P). Turning a numbered knob to 0 removes that row from every pin in it. The lettered knob sets the starting point that pinned voltages move up or down; with nothing pinned it is the whole setting. patch_matrix records both links as level_param and offset_param.

midi.note: No MIDI and no digital control of any kind. External control is by voltages through the HI LEVEL inputs and the KEYBOARD socket.

source_inconsistencies: Maximum envelope repetition rate is 60 Hz in the specification and 'about 50 Hz' in the Envelope Shaper text.
Osc 3's lower limit is 0.025 Hz (40 s) in the text and 0.015 Hz (65 s) at dial 0 in the calibration table, which notes the extreme varies. A later panel prints 0.05 Hz.
Osc 1 and 2 are 1 Hz to 10 kHz in the text; the calibration table runs 0.6 Hz to 16.75 kHz at the dial ends, marked as possibly outside tolerance.
The matrix walkthrough lists a pin as B10 where its diagram shows D10 (filter into envelope shaper); the reverb example prints B13 where D13 is meant.

Wikipedia and several retailers call the filter 24 dB/octave; the manual specifies 12 dB in the first octave and 18 dB/octave beyond. Not a contradiction: Sound On Sound reports that EMS changed the filter to 24 dB/octave in 1974, after the Mk 1.

A Mk 2 matrix legend prints Output ch1, meter, Output ch2 across columns A to C, while the Mk 1 manual and panel put the meter on A and the outputs on B and C. Portabella confirms the meter moved to column B on the Mk 2; this file keeps the Mk 1 order.
Sound On Sound's 'All About EMS' places Osc 1 on row 3 and output channel 1 on column A. That is the Mk 2 layout; on the Mk 1 they are rows 1 and 2 and column B.
Red pins are given as 2% tolerance by Sound On Sound and Hinton Instruments, and 1% by forum posters describing modern replacements.

modelling_gaps.detail: The matrix sums through 2.7 kohm into 10 kohm inputs with no buffering, so the gain of any pin depends on every other pin in its column and row. The file records the values; a simulation would need to solve the resistor network.

Modelled on the Mk 1 (1969 to about 1972), as the manual describes it. The Mk 2 differs: rows 1 and 2 become Output ch 1 and 2, rows 3 and 4 carry Osc 1 and Osc 2 as single mixed outputs, the meter moves to column B and output channel 1 to column A, and row 16 doubles as a sequencer input from Jones pin 8 (selected by clicking the vertical RANGE knob to 'seq'). From 1974 the filter became 24 dB/octave. Mk 1 units used a GE PA234 power amplifier IC and an inexpensive Japanese spring tank; new Cornwall units use an Accutronics tank. None of this is modelled here.

Many surviving units carry EMS or third-party modifications that are not part of a stock Mk 1 and are not modelled: HI/LO range switches on Osc 2 and 3, an envelope trigger source switch (keyboard socket or external gate), input channel SI/MULT switches, voltage-controlled shape jacks for the three oscillators, a dual patchable inverter, a four-way multiple, extra input channels with an EXT CV/STICK switch, oscillator sync, matrix buffering, and Mk 2 matrices rewired to Mk 1 rows.
The VCS3 is famous for drift. Nothing in the manual quantifies it beyond warm-up and calibration advice.
Slopes and Q are specified; the diode-ladder character, the sine shaper's curve and the pulse width at each shape setting are not.
There is nothing digital. The midi section is empty; every patch is pins plus knob positions, which example_patches records where the manual gives them.
